name: The Gülhane London Plane
story: A London plane cannot be much older than about 350 years, because the hybrid did not exist before roughly 1670. This one, at about 285, comfortably fits, which is not true of every tree the Turkish registry files under that name. Two of Istanbul's own registered giants carry the same label at ages that would make the hybrid older than itself; here the arithmetic works, and the identification is plausible rather than proven. Turkey's national monumental tree registry records it at 33 metres tall with a trunk 170 centimetres across and an age of 277 years. Istanbul's metropolitan municipality publishes its own page for this exact tree, with identical measurements, saying it has stood in Gülhane Park since 1741. The two numbers add up to 2018, so both trace to one survey rather than two independent measurements. Two official bodies, one field visit, worth knowing. For most of its life nobody could walk past it. Gülhane was the outer garden of Topkapı Palace, court ground rather than public space, until it opened in 1912 as Istanbul's first public park. The tree was already 170 years old by then. It stands about 40 metres from a registered nettle tree of similar age, 350 metres from the Topkapı courtyard plane and 550 metres from the Taşlı Çınar, which makes this the tightest cluster on Istanbul's list.

name: The Gülhane Nettle Tree
story: Istanbul protects this tree by name, which is unusual for a species most cities treat as background. The Mediterranean hackberry, çitlembik in Turkish, normally gets planted for shade and forgotten. This one is 23 metres tall with a trunk 145 centimetres across, and it holds a place on Turkey's national monumental tree registry at an age of 259 years, with the city's own municipal tree project publishing a page for it saying it has stood in Gülhane Park since 1759. Those two figures resolve to the same year, 2018, so the national register and the city are reporting one survey between them rather than two separate measurements. That is worth stating. What makes the number credible anyway is the species: Celtis australis is a tough, long-lived tree in Anatolian conditions, so 265 years is physically ordinary for it, which is more than can be said for some of the plane ages in the same register. It stands roughly 40 metres from the registered London plane in the same park, and the pair are the reason to come. Gülhane was Topkapı's outer palace garden and stayed closed to the public until 1912, so this tree spent its first century and a half inside a court garden and its last hundred years among people eating simit under it. The Topkapı courtyard plane is 300 metres away.

name: The Topkapı Palace Yew

location.address: Topkapı Palace, Fourth Courtyard area, Cankurtaran, Fatih, Istanbul

story: For a yew, three centuries is early middle age. This one, in the Fourth Courtyard of Topkapı Palace, is registered at 314 years, 13 metres tall with a trunk 103 centimetres across and a crown 12 metres wide, which by the standards of a species that can run to millennia makes it a young adult with a long career ahead. The government record has quirks worth naming. Two views of the same database give the age as 314 and 310, a four-year drift, and one of them files the tree under a district hundreds of kilometres away in Ankara province while its own description talks about Topkapı, which is a clerical slip rather than a doubt about where the tree is. Separately, an independent field survey measured three yews in this courtyard, two of them 3.26 and 3.09 metres around, and photographed them in December 2014. That is the freshest direct evidence of them standing that this entry rests on, and it is now twelve years old. Unlike the other trees on this list, it costs money. The Fourth Courtyard was the sultan's private terrace garden, above the Golden Horn beside the Baghdad Kiosk that Murad IV built in 1639, and reaching it needs a Topkapı Palace museum ticket. The free trees of Gülhane Park are 550 metres downhill.
